# Discussion

{{< meta libname >}} demonstrates that the complete reaction-template application workflow can be transferred to GPUs without sacrificing consistency of the generated precursors. Its CUDA and Metal backends produced identical outputs, showed high agreement with established engines, and supported both route replay and exhaustive depth-two expansion. These findings extend GPU acceleration beyond substructure matching alone and show that GPU-generated precursors can be reused across successive retrosynthetic steps. At the same time, the rapid growth of the molecular frontier shows that faster reaction application does not remove the need for effective search, filtering, and deduplication.

The exhaustive expansion showed that {{< meta libname >}} can generate and retain large sets of alternative transformations, but it also illustrated why reaction application alone does not define a search strategy. {{< meta libname >}} therefore separates reaction application from the choice of which molecule or partial route to expand. This design allows guided AND/OR search methods to use the same precursor and provenance records while applying their own heuristics. By reducing the cost of generating each set of alternatives, {{< meta libname >}} may allow an integrated planner to expand more nodes, retain more candidate disconnections, or rank successful applications after their precursor structures have been generated.

Beyond route expansion, fast enumeration may support a more explicit assessment of selectivity and competing reactions. A successful template application shows only that the encoded graph transformation can be performed; it does not establish that the intended reaction would dominate experimentally. Pairing each retrosynthetic template with a corresponding forward rule would allow the generated precursors to be tested for alternative reactive sites, competing transformations, and repeated functionalization. These checks could flag reactions that require closer evaluation before they are retained in a route.

The same framework could also account for molecular contexts in which an otherwise valid transformation should be rejected or penalized. Such contexts could be encoded as negative application conditions—structural patterns that identify incompatible functional groups or local environments. A functional-group vocabulary such as SMARTS-RX, which contains 406 curated descriptors [@smartsrx2025], could provide many of the required patterns. However, SMARTS-RX does not specify which groups interfere with which reactions; implementing this extension would therefore require curating and validating the associations between retrosynthetic templates, forward rules, and reaction-specific negative conditions.

With these extensions, {{< meta libname >}} could evaluate not only whether a template produces a valid molecular graph, corresponding to Solv-1 in the Solv-N framework, but also whether the intended reaction remains plausible in the presence of alternative sites and transformations (Solv-2) [@morgunov2026syntax]. These checks are not included in the current implementation. A future study could combine fast exhaustive reaction application with curated forward rules and negative application conditions and test whether this approach improves route-level chemical plausibility using a benchmark such as URSA [@zagribelnyy2026ursa].


# Conclusions

{{< meta libname >}} provides an open-source implementation of the complete reaction-template application pipeline for GPU and parallel CPU execution. It covers matching, graph transformation, connected-component analysis, precursor generation, chemical-property updates, deduplication, and provenance recording through a common interface. {{< meta libname >}}, tested with CUDA, Metal, and parallel CPU execution, generated consistent precursor outcomes and agreed with RDChiral for 98.3% of nearly 770 000 confirmed molecule–template pairs. Template-guided replay recovered 99.7% of 10 000 reference routes, while exhaustive depth-two expansion recovered the reference route for 99.7% of targets. These results show that {{< meta libname >}} generates precursors that can be used across successive retrosynthetic steps. They also show that substructure matching accounts for only a small part of the complete workflow, with precursor construction, chemical-property perception, molecular-key generation, deduplication, and orchestration determining most of its cost. {{< meta libname >}} therefore provides reusable infrastructure for retrosynthetic planning and other high-throughput cheminformatics applications.
